PART 7 — Boundaries in Each Relationship

What a boundary is. A boundary describes what I will do or allow, not what I can make you do (Cloud & Townsend's widely used framing). "If you shout, I will leave the room and come back when we can talk calmly" is a boundary. "You must stop shouting" is a demand. Boundaries are for keeping love honest, not for punishing.

7.1 The Three-Part Response (for Either Side)

StepWhat it doesExample
1. Acknowledge the love or fear underneathLowers defence; the person feels seen"I know you say this because you worry about me."
2. State the decision or limit plainlyStays with "I," not "you must""I have decided to take the job. I'm not asking for permission."
3. Stay relational and name the consequence, if anyKeeps the door open; limits are not punishment"I'd love your support. I won't discuss it every day, but I'll gladly tell you how it's going."

7.2 Parents of Minor Children

Parents have real, God-given authority and responsibility for children (Eph 6:1-4; Prov 22:6). The task is to use it as training toward freedom, so that control shrinks as the child's capacity grows.

LegitimateWhere care turns controlWhat to do instead
Non-negotiable safety rules (road, internet, strangers, substances)Treating preferences and image as safetySeparate three lists: non-negotiable (safety, values with reasons), negotiable, and theirs to choose (friends' styles, hobbies, many tastes)
Consequences for broken rulesLove withdrawal; humiliation; comparisons; "after all I've done"Consequences that are predictable, proportionate and linked to the behaviour; affection stays steady
Guiding career and educationChoosing the child's life path; marks as the measure of worthExplore strengths together; reasons and information, then increasing say as they mature
Monitoring young childrenReading a teen's every message "out of love"Transparent, age-appropriate oversight that is explained and reduced as trust grows
CorrectionProvoking anger and discouragement (Eph 6:4; Col 3:21)Correct the behaviour, never the child's worth; repair quickly after harsh moments, with an apology if needed

Script (teenager): "I'm not saying yes to this trip. My reason is [the specific risk], and I'd rather explain than just say no. I might be wrong, so tell me what you think. If we can make a plan that deals with [the risk], I'm willing to reconsider."

7.3 Parents of Adult Children

The role shifts from manager to consultant, then friend. An adult may make decisions you consider unwise: career, marriage, faith, money, place of residence.

LegitimateWhere care turns controlWhat to do instead
Sharing concern or experienceRepeating it, or making support conditional on agreement"Do you want my view?" Say it once; then "it's your decision and I'm with you"
Deciding what you will fund or doUsing money, inheritance or approval as leverage to force choicesState your limits openly and consistently; don't use gifts as a leash, and don't withdraw love to teach a lesson
Hoping for a certain marriage, faith or careerSilence, guilt, comparisons, rejection of the spouse or grandchildrenWelcome the person they chose; let the relationship earn trust over time
Helping in genuine needRescuing from every consequence; hoveringHelp that builds capacity (a plan, a loan with terms, a ride to counselling) rather than removing the consequence

Script (parent to adult son): "I'm worried about this job change, and I wanted you to hear it from me once. It's your life and your decision. I'll still be at the table on Sunday, and if you want a sounding board, I'm here."

7.4 Adult Children With Controlling Parents

Scripture says "honour your father and mother" (kabed: give weight to) and also that a man "leaves (azab) his father and mother" to form a new household (Gen 2:24). Honour is lifelong respect and care; it is not unlimited obedience or surrender of your conscience.

SituationWhat may helpScript
Guilt: "After all we sacrificed"Thank genuinely without accepting the debt as a lever; decide from conscience, not from guilt"I'm deeply grateful, and I'll always honour you. That doesn't mean I can make this decision your way."
Marriage or career pressureListen, explain once, decide, inform; don't ask permission you aren't willing to accept a "no" to"I've decided. I'd love your blessing, but I'm going ahead either way."
Intrusion into spouse/homeAgree boundaries with your spouse first; present them together"Visits happen when we've arranged them. Decisions about our home are ours."
Silent treatment or anger when you refuseStay warm and consistent; do not chase, plead or retaliate; keep contact at a level you can sustain"I'll call on Sunday. When you're ready to talk calmly, I'm here."
Financial stringsBe honest about what you can accept; separate gifts from obligations"Thank you, but I can't accept money with conditions about my choices."
Abusive or intimidating behaviourLimit or pause contact; involve a counsellor or trusted third party; safety first (Part 8)"I will end this call if there is shouting. I'll try again next week."

Expect pushback and waves of guilt: when a long-standing pattern is changed, the system often escalates before it settles ("the extinction burst" in behavioural terms). Consistent, kind boundaries usually matter more than any single script.

7.5 Spouses

Marriage is a covenant between two adults, neither of whom owns the other. Scripture speaks of mutual regard (Eph 5:21; 1 Pet 3:7), and even in sexual intimacy of authority that is mutual and by agreement (1 Cor 7:3-5). It does not grant either a right to monitor, isolate or coerce.

Common "love" behaviourWhat it can becomeA healthy alternative
"I just want to know where you are."Constant tracking, checking phone, demands to explainAgreed, mutual transparency, not one-sided surveillance; assume good faith
"I'm jealous because I love you."Limiting friends, family, work, clothesName the insecurity ("I feel threatened and I'm working on it"); don't assign the cure to the spouse
"We share everything."One partner controls all money and informationJoint planning and transparency about finances, with real access for both
"I know what's best for the family."Unilateral major decisions; "God told me"Decide together; listen to the objection as information, not rebellion
Moods, silence, anger as pressureThe household walking on eggshellsTake a time-out, return and talk; name the need

Script (spouse): "When I'm asked to explain where I've been, I feel watched, not loved. I understand that you feel anxious when I'm late. What if I text when I'm leaving, and we work on the worry together, but I don't want to be checked on?"

If you are afraid of your partner (fear of anger or violence, being cut off from family and friends, money and phone controlled, threats, forced sex or self-harm threats used to keep you), this is beyond a "communication problem." Tell a trusted person; consider a counsellor, women's organisation or lawyer; make a safety plan. In India: 112 (emergency), 181 (women's helpline). Please verify the numbers locally; they can change. The relational gospel does not require you to "stay and absorb" harm; safety is not a failure of love.

7.6 Friends, Siblings, Leaders and Churches

RelationshipLegitimateRed flagsBoundary
Friends and siblingsHonest concern; accountability the person choseUltimatums; triangulating others; surveillanceSay it once; leave the choice with them; keep the friendship
Pastors/leadersTeaching, care, accountability that is voluntary and transparent"Questioning is rebellion"; "God told me"; control of marriage, money, friends; punishment for leavingAuthority serves (Matt 20:25-28); you may ask questions, seek second opinions, and leave
Caregivers of the sick/elderlySafety, medical decisions where capacity is limitedOverriding a capable person's wishesInclude them in decisions as far as possible

PART 8 — Hard Cases and When Intervening Is Love

The third way is not "never step in." Some situations call for protective action. The test is below.

8.1 When Stronger Action Can Be Loving

Stronger intervention may be appropriate when all or most of these apply: (1) the harm is serious and hard to reverse (life, safety, serious injury, lasting legal or medical consequences); (2) the person is a child, or cannot make a free and informed choice (acute crisis, dementia, severe intoxication, or being coerced by someone else); (3) there is a third party at risk; (4) gentler steps have been tried or there is no time; and (5) you use the least restrictive means and involve appropriate professionals or authorities. It is protection, not victory, and it aims at restoring the person's capacity to choose.

SituationNot control; protective love may look likeCaution
Suicidal statements or self-harmTake it seriously; stay with them; remove means if possible; contact emergency services or a crisis line; connect to professional careDon't promise secrecy; don't argue them out of their pain; don't handle alone
AddictionHonest conversation; boundaries about money, housing and lying; encourage treatment; use professional intervention models; support family members tooRescuing and bailing out feeds it; threats and ultimatums rarely work if they are not consistently followed through
Child at riskStep in; involve childcare services if necessarySafety of the child outweighs a parent's feelings or family image
Elderly parent with dementiaTake decisions on safety, finance and driving, with respect for dignityThe aim is protection of a person with reduced capacity, not obedience
Adult in a risky relationship (not abuse yet)Keep contact; tell the truth once; stay a safe person to come back toUltimatums or cutting off often push the person toward the risky partner and away from you
Adult in an abusive relationshipBelieve them; don't pressure them to leave on your timetable; share resources; keep the door open; help with a safety planLeaving is often the most dangerous time; they need to decide with support
Cult-like group or high-control churchKeep the relationship; ask questions rather than attack the leader; keep them connected to the outside worldForced removal can backfire; consult those experienced in spiritual abuse

If someone is in immediate danger, contact emergency services (112 in India). For emotional distress or suicidal thoughts, India's Tele-MANAS service (14416) and Childline (1098, for children) are published national lines; please verify numbers and availability locally. If you yourself are being controlled or abused, speak to a trusted person or professional. This study cannot replace them.

PART 9 — If I Am the One Who Controls

You may be reading this and recognise yourself. That recognition is not condemnation; it is the doorway to repair (compare the earlier studies on shame and on repentance). The relational gospel starts from acceptance: "Nothing can separate us from the love of God" (Rom 8:38-39). You can look at this without being destroyed by it.

9.1 Ten Self-Questions

  1. What exactly am I afraid will happen if they choose differently?
  2. If that happened, what would it say about me? (That is usually the I-am-not.)
  3. Whose peace am I protecting, mine or theirs?
  4. Can they say "no" to me and still feel loved?
  5. Do I use guilt, silence, comparison, money or God's name to move them?
  6. Have I given my reasons, and listened to theirs, as if I might be wrong?
  7. Am I treating an adult as a child, or a preference as a danger?
  8. Is my love the same when they obey and when they don't?
  9. What did I learn about love from my own family?
  10. If they stopped needing me tomorrow, who would I be?

9.2 Turning Control Sentences into Honest Ones

Control sentenceHonest, vulnerable sentence
"You can't go. It's not safe.""I'm scared when you go. I know that's mine to manage. Can we plan how you'll keep in touch?"
"After all I've done for you…""I gave gladly, and I also feel unseen. I'd love to feel appreciated, but you owe me nothing."
"If you loved me, you would…""I feel insecure about us, and I'm working on that; it isn't a test for you."
"I know what's best for you.""Here's what I see, and I may be wrong. What do you think?"
(silence and cold shoulder)"I'm hurt and need an hour; then I'd like to talk."

9.3 Steps of Change

  1. Name it without self-hatred. "I have been using fear and pressure and calling it love."
  2. Find the fear and the I-am-not. Write it down; bring it to the Father and to a counsellor or trusted friend.
  3. Grieve what was missing. Often it is what you needed and did not receive.
  4. Receive what you were looking for. Security, significance and belonging come first as gifts (the earlier studies on union and on needs).
  5. Practise tolerating uncertainty. Anxiety rises when you stop controlling; let it pass without acting on it. This is the hardest and most important skill.
  6. Apologise specifically and offer repair (see More Than "Sorry"): name the tactics, ask what it was like, and do not demand forgiveness.
  7. Change the pattern and be accountable. Ask someone to tell you when they see control returning; expect slow rebuilding of trust.
  8. Seek professional help if control involves intimidation, violence, or a long pattern that you cannot stop.
